Chapter on "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" (Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim)

Ibn ʿUmar said: It was revealed at the beginning of every surah.

The scholars differed over whether it is a complete verse (ayah) or not, and on this there are two reports from Ahmad.

They also differed over whether it is part of al-Fatihah or not, and on this too there are two reports from Ahmad.

As for the one who holds that it is part of al-Fatihah, he makes its recitation obligatory in the prayer if he holds that al-Fatihah is obligatory. As for the one who does not regard it as part of al-Fatihah, he says that reciting it in the prayer is a sunnah.

Malik alone does not recommend reciting it in the prayer.

They differed concerning reciting it aloud (al-jahr) in the prayer, in those prayers where the recitation is audible. A group transmitted from Ahmad that it is not sunnah to recite it aloud, and this is the view of Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthman, ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud, ʿAmmar ibn Yasir, Ibn Mughaffal, Ibn al-Zubayr, and Ibn ʿAbbas. It was also held by senior Successors (tabiʿun) and those after them: al-Hasan, al-Shaʿbi, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim, Qatadah, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, al-Aʿmash, Sufyan al-Thawri, Malik, Abu Hanifah, and Abu ʿUbayd, among others.

Al-Shafiʿi held that reciting it aloud is sunnah, and this is also narrated from Muʿawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, ʿAta', Tawus, and Mujahid.

As for its explanation:

His saying "Bismillah" is an abbreviation, as if he said: "I begin with the name of Allah," or: "I began with the name of Allah."

The word "ism" (name) has five dialectal forms: "ism" with a kasrah on the alif; "usm" with a dammah on the alif when you begin with it; "sim" with a kasrah on the sin; "sum" with a dammah on the sin; and "sama".

The poet said:

May Allah name you a blessed name (sumaan mubarakan), by which Allah has preferred you with preference.

And they recited:

With the name of the One whose mark (simuhu) is in every surah.

Al-Farra' said: Some of Qays say "simuhu," meaning "ismuhu," and some of Qudaʿah say "sumuhu."

One of them recited to me:

Our year's first-comer pleased us, called Abu al-Samh, and his name (sumuhu) is Qirdab.

Al-Qirdab means "the cutter"; one says "a sword that is qirdab."

The scholars differed concerning the name of Allah which is "Allah":

Some said it is derived (mushtaqq), and others said it is a proper name (ʿalam) and not derived.

On this there are two reports from al-Khalil:

One: that it is not derived, and it is not permissible to drop the alif and lam from it, as it is permissible with al-Rahman.

The second, which Sibawayh transmitted from him: that it is derived.

Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi mentioned from some scholars that its root in speech is derived from: "alaha al-rajulu ya'lahu," meaning: when a man sought refuge with someone from a matter that befell him.

So "alaha" means he granted him protection and security, and so He was named "ilah" just as a man is named "imam."

Others said: its root is "walaha" (to be bewildered/devoted). The waw was changed to a hamzah, and it became "ilah," as they said "wisadah" and "isadah," and "wishah" and "ishah."

It is also derived from "al-walah" (passionate longing), because the hearts of servants are devoted to Him, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then when harm touches you, to Him you cry out﴾ [al-Nahl: 53].

The analogical form would have been "ma'luh" (one who is worshipped), as "ma'bud" is formed, but they deviated from this pattern so that it would become a proper name, just as they said "kitab" for what is written and "hisab" for what is counted.

Some said: its root is from "alaha al-rajulu ya'lahu," meaning he was bewildered, because hearts are bewildered when reflecting on His greatness.

It is related from some philologists: "alaha al-rajulu ya'lahu ilahatan," meaning: he worshipped, ya'bud ʿibadah.

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said concerning the verse ﴿and [Pharaoh] abandon you and your gods (aalihatak)﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 127]: that is, your worship.

He said: and al-taʾalluh means worship (al-taʿabbud).

Ru'bah said:

By Allah, the excellence of the dancing girls who sway, they glorified and said "istirja'" for one who worships me (ta'allahi).

So the meaning of "ilah" is "the one worshipped."

As for "al-Rahman":

The majority held that it is derived from "al-rahmah" (mercy), formed for intensity, and its meaning is: the One possessing a mercy for which there is no equal.

The pattern fa'lan in their speech denotes intensity, for they say of one who is extremely full: "mal'an," and of one extremely sated: "sab'an."

Al-Khattabi said: "al-Rahman" is the One possessing all-encompassing mercy, which embraced creation in their provisions and their welfare, and which extended to both the believer and the disbeliever.

And "al-Rahim" is specific to the believers.

The Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And He is ever Merciful to the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 43].

And "al-Rahim" carries the meaning of "al-Rahim" (the one who shows mercy).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 1, verse 2:

(p-10) Surat al-Fatiha.

Abu Hurayra narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited Umm al-Qur'an to him, and he said: 'By Him in Whose hand is my soul, there has not been sent down in the Torah, nor in the Gospel, nor in the Psalms, nor in the Furqan (Criterion, i.e. the Qur'an) anything like it. It is the seven oft-repeated (al-sab' al-mathani) and the Great Qur'an which you have been given.'"

Among its names is al-Fatiha (the Opening), because the Book is opened with it in recitation and in writing.

Among its names is Umm al-Qur'an and Umm al-Kitab (the Mother of the Qur'an and the Mother of the Book), because it precedes the Book and takes precedence over it.

Among its names is al-Sab' al-Mathani (the Seven Oft-Repeated), and it was so named for what we will explain in (al-Hijr), God willing.

The scholars differed concerning its revelation, into two views.

The first: that it is Meccan. This is narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliya, Qatada, and Abu Maysara.

The second: that it is Medinan. This is narrated from Abu Hurayra, Mujahid, Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, and 'Ata al-Khurasani. And from Ibn 'Abbas, there are two reports like both views.

Section

As for its interpretation:

﴿Al-hamdu﴾ is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), and (lillahi) is the predicate (khabar).

The meaning: praise is established and settled for Allah.

The majority read the lam of (lillahi) with a kasra, while Ibn 'Abla read it with a damma. Al-Farra' said: it is the dialect of some of the Banu Rabi'a. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read (al-hamda) with a fatha on the dal and (lillahi) with a kasra on the lam. Abu Nahik read both the dal and the lam with a kasra.

Know that al-hamd is praise of the one praised, and shukr (thanks) shares it, except that there is a difference between them: al-hamd may occur as an initiation of praise, whereas shukr does not occur except in return for a favour. It has also been said: its wording is that of a report, but its meaning is a command, so its implied sense is: "Say: al-hamdu lillah."

Ibn Qutayba said: al-hamd is praising a man for what is in him of generosity, noble lineage, courage, and the like.

And shukr is praising him for a kindness he has bestowed, and hamd may be placed in the position of shukr, so one says: "I praised him (hamidtuhu) for his kindness to me," just as one says: "I thanked him (shakartu lahu) for his courage."

As for (al-Rabb), it means the Owner, and this name is not mentioned in reference to a created being except with an added genitive, so one says: "This is the master (rabb) of the house, and the master of the slave."

It has also been said: it is derived from tarbiya (nurturing).

Our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi said: one says: "Rabb fulan sani'atahu yarubbuha rabban," meaning when he completes and improves it; so he is a rabb and a rabb. 

The poet said:

"Yurabbi alladhi ya'ti min al-khayri innahu / idha su'ila al-ma'ruf zada wa tammama"

He said: al-Rabb is used in three senses.

One: the Owner. One says: rabb al-dar (the owner of the house).

The second: the Reformer, as one says: rabb al-shay' (the one who sets a thing right).

The third: the lord who is obeyed, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So he will give his lord (rabbahu) wine to drink﴾ [Yusuf: 41].

The majority read the ba' of "rabbin" with a kasra. Abu al-'Aliya, Ibn al-Sumayfa', and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it with a fatha.

Abu Razin al-Uqayli, al-Rabi' ibn Khaythum, and Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read it with a damma.

(p-12) As for (al-'alamin), it is the plural of 'alam, and according to the grammarians it is a name for creation from its beginning to its end. They have called the people of the present age 'alam.

Al-Hutay'a said:

"Tanahha fajlisi minni ba'idan / arah Allahu minka al-'alamina"

As for the people of rational inquiry (ahl al-nazar), 'alam is a name that applies to the whole originated cosmos, consisting of the sphere, the heaven, the earth, and what lies between them.

Concerning the derivation of 'alam there are two views.

The first: that it is from 'ilm (knowledge), and this strengthens the view of the linguists.

The second: that it is from 'alama (sign), and this strengthens the view of the rational inquirers, for it is named thus among them because it points to its Creator.

Regarding the meaning of "al-'alamin" here, the exegetes have five views:

The first: all creation, the heavens and the earths and what is in them and between them. Narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: every living being that crawls upon the face of the earth. Narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that they are the jinn and mankind. Also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid and Muqatil said so.

The fourth: that they are the jinn, mankind, and the angels. Also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Qutayba chose it.

The fifth: that they are the angels. Also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

Allah's saying: ﴿Ar-Rahmani r-Rahim﴾ (The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful).

Abu al-Aliyah, Ibn al-Sumaifa'(Ibn al-Sumaifa') and Isa ibn Umar read both words in the accusative (naṣb). Abu Razin al-Uqaili, al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham and Abu Imran al-Jawni read both in the nominative (raf').

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 1, verse 4:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾.

ʿĀṣim, al-Kisāʾī, Khalaf and Yaʿqūb read "Mālik" with an alif. Ibn al-Samayfaʿ and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read likewise, except that they put the kāf in the accusative (Mālika).

Abū Hurayra and ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī read "Malk" with the lām sukūn and no alif, with the kāf kasra. Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī and al-Shaʿbī read "Malika" with the lām kasra and the kāf accusative, without an alif.

Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, ʿĀʾisha and Muwarriq al-ʿIjlī read "Maluk" in the same manner, except that they put the kāf in the nominative (Malaku, i.e. Malukun).

Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Abū Rajāʾ al-ʿUṭāridī read "Malīk" with a yā' after the lām, the kāf kasra, and without an alif.

ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ read likewise, except that he put a ḍamma on the kāf.

Abū Ḥanīfa and Abū Ḥaywa read "Malaka" as a past-tense verb, and "yawma" with a fatḥa (accusative).

ʿAbd al-Wārith related from Abū ʿAmr the sukūn of the lām. The well-known reading from Abū ʿAmr and the majority of the readers is "Maliki" with a fatḥa on the mīm and a kasra on the lām, and it is the more evident in praise, because every king is a master (mālik), but not every master is a king.

Regarding "al-Dīn" here there are two views:

The first: that it means the reckoning. This is the saying of Ibn Masʿūd.

The second: that it means the recompense. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbās. And since Allah, mighty and majestic, affirmed in His saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ that He is the Master of this world, He indicated by His saying ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ that He is the Master of the Hereafter.

It was also said: He singled out the Day of Judgment because on that day He alone holds the judgment over His creation.

(p-14) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thee do we worship﴾.

Al-Hasan, Abu al-Mutawakkil and Abu Mijlaz read "yu'badu" (it is worshipped), with a damma on the yā' and a fatḥa on the bā'.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning is: "Say, O Muhammad: Thee is worshipped." The Arabs shift from the third person (ghayba) to the second person (khitab), and from the second person to the third person, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when you were in the ship and they sailed with them﴾ [Yunus: 32], and His saying: ﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink. Indeed, this has been for you a reward﴾ [al-Insan/al-Dahr: 21-22]. 

Labid said:

Her soul complains to me, distressed, while she has preserved you seven and seventy years over.

There are three opinions regarding the intended meaning of this worship (ʿibadah, "worship").

The first: that it means tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness).
This is narrated from ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas, along with others.

The second: that it means obedience (ta'ah), as in His saying: ﴿Do not worship Satan﴾ [Ya Sin: 60].

The third: that both mean supplication (du'a'), as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disdain My worship﴾ [Ghafir: 60].

ۘ**Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 1, verse 6**

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿اهْدِنا﴾ فِيهِ أرْبَعَةُ أقْوالٍ:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Guide us﴾ (ihdina). There are four opinions concerning it:

أحَدُها: ثَبِّتْنا. قالَهُ عَلِيٌّ، وأُبِيُّ. والثّانِي: أرْشِدْنا. والثّالِثُ: وُفِّقْنا. والرّابِعُ: ألْهِمْنا. رُوِيَتْ هَذِهِ الثَّلاثَةُ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ.

The first: "Make us firm." This was said by ʿAli and Ubayy. The second: "Show us the way." The third: "Grant us success." The fourth: "Inspire us." These three were related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

**

(وَالصِّراطَ) الطَّرِيقُ. ويُقالُ: إنَّ أصْلَهُ بِالسِّينِ، لِأنَّهُ مِنَ " الِاسْتِراطِ " وهُوَ: الِابْتِلاعُ فالسِّراطُ كَأنَّهُ يَسْتَرِطُ المارِّينَ عَلَيْهِ، فَمَن قَرَأ بِالسِّينِ، كَمُجاهِدٍ، وابْنِ مُحَيْصِنٍ، ويَعْقُوبَ، فَعَلى أصْلِ الكَلِمَةِ، ومَن قَرَأ بِالصّادِّ، كَأبِي عَمْرٍو، والجُمْهُورِ، فَلِأنَّها أخَفُّ عَلى اللِّسانِ، ومَن قَرَأ بِالزّايِ، كَرِوايَةِ الأصْمَعِيِّ عَنْ أبِي عَمْرٍو، واحْتَجَّ بِقَوْلِ العَرَبِ: "سَقْرٌ وزَقْرٌ"، ورُوِيَ (p-١٥)عَنْ حَمْزَةَ: إشْمامُ السِّينِ زايًا، ورُوِيَ عَنْهُ أنَّهُ تَلَفَّظَ بِالصِّراطِ بَيْنَ الصّادِ والزّايِ.

(Al-ṣirāṭa) means "the path." It is said that its original form is with the letter sīn, because it derives from "al-istirāṭ," which means "swallowing." So the ṣirāṭ is as if it swallows those who pass along it. Whoever recites it with sīn, like Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, and Yaʿqub, does so according to the original root of the word. Whoever recites it with ṣād, like Abu ʿAmr and the majority, does so because it is lighter on the tongue. Whoever recites it with zāy, as in the transmission of al-Asmaʿi from Abu ʿAmr, cites the Arabic saying "saqr wa zaqr" as evidence. It is related from Hamza that he pronounced the sīn with a zāy-like sound (ishmām), and it is also related from him that he pronounced aṣ-ṣirāṭ between ṣād and zāy.

قالَ الفَرّاءُ: اللُّغَةُ الجَيِّدَةُ بِالصّادِّ، وهي لُغَةُ قُرَيْشٍ الأُولى، وعامَّةُ العَرَبِ يَجْعَلُونَها سِينًا، وبَعْضُ قَيْسٍ يَشُمُّونَ الصّادَ، فَيَقُولُ "الصِّراطَ" بَيْنَ الصّادِ والسِّينِ، وكانَ حَمْزَةُ يَقْرَأُ "الزِّراطَ" بِالزّايِ، وهي لُغَةٌ لِعُذْرَةٍ وكَلْبٍ وبَنِي القَيْنِ. يَقُولُونَ في [أصْدَقُ ] أزْدَقُ.

Al-Farra' said: The good dialect uses ṣād, and it is the primary dialect of Quraysh. Most Arabs make it sīn, and some of Qays give the ṣād a sīn-like coloring (ishmām), so they say "aṣ-ṣirāṭa" between ṣād and sīn. Hamza used to recite "az-zirāṭa" with zāy, and this is a dialect of ʿUdhra, Kalb, and Banu al-Qayn. They say "azdaq" for [aṣdaq].

وَفِي المُرادِ بِالصِّراطِ هاهُنا أرْبَعَةُ أقْوالٍ.

As for what is meant by aṣ-ṣirāṭ here, there are four opinions.

أحَدُها: أنَّهُ كِتابُ اللَّهِ، رَواهُ عَلِيٌّ عَنِ النَّبِيِّ ﷺ .

The first: that it is the Book of God. ʿAli related this from the Prophet (ﷺ).

والثّانِي: أنَّهُ دِينُ الإسْلامِ. قالَهُ ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ، وابْنُ عَبّاسٍ، والحُسْنُ، وأبُو العالِيَةِ في آَخَرِينَ.

The second: that it is the religion of Islam. This was said by Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Abu al-ʿAliya, and others.

والثّالِثُ: أنَّهُ الطَّرِيقُ الهادِي إلى دِينِ اللَّهِ، رَواهُ أبُو صالِحٍ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ، وبِهِ قالَ مُجاهِدٌ.

The third: that it is the path that leads to the religion of God. Abu Salih related this from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Mujahid said likewise.

والرّابِعُ: أنَّهُ طَرِيقُ الجَنَّةِ، نُقِلَ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ أيْضًا. فَإنْ قِيلَ: ما مَعْنى سُؤالِ المُسْلِمِينَ الهِدايَةَ وهم مُهْتَدُونَ؟ فَفِيهِ ثَلاثَةُ أجْوِبَةٍ:

The fourth: that it is the path to Paradise, also related from Ibn ʿAbbas. If it is asked: what is the meaning of Muslims asking for guidance when they are already guided? There are three answers to this.

أحَدُها: أنَّ المَعْنى: اهْدِنا لُزُومَ الصِّراطَ، فَحَذَفَ اللُّزُومَ. قالَهُ ابْنُ الأنْبارِيِّ.

The first: the meaning is "Guide us to adhere to the path," and the word "adherence" is omitted. This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

والثّانِي: أنَّ المَعْنى: ثَبِّتْنا عَلى الهُدى، تَقُولُ العَرَبُ لِلْقائِمِ: قُمْ حَتّى آَتِيَكَ، أيِ: اثْبُتْ عَلى حالِكَ.

The second: the meaning is "Make us firm upon guidance," as the Arabs say to one who is standing, "Stay until I come to you," meaning: remain in your state.

والثّالِثُ: أنَّ المَعْنى: زِدْنا هُدًى.

The third: the meaning is "Increase us in guidance."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 1, verse 7:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿Of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾

Ibn 'Abbas said: They are the Prophets, the truthful (al-siddiqun), the martyrs, and the righteous. Most of the readers recited "'alayhim" with a kasra on the ha' (hā'), and likewise "ladayhim" and "ilayhim"; Hamzah recited them with a damma. Ibn Kathir would join the damma of the mim with a waw. Ibn al-Anbari said: The linguists have recorded ten dialectal forms of "'alayhim," and it has been recited in most of them: "'alayhum" with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the mim; "'alayhim" with a kasra on the ha' and a sukun on the mim; "'alayhimi" with a kasra on the ha' and the mim, and a ya' added after the kasra; "'alayhimu" with a kasra on the ha' and a damma on the mim, with a waw added after the damma; "'alayhumu" with a damma on the ha' and the mim, with a waw inserted after the mim; and "'alayhum" with a damma on the ha' and the mim without an added waw. These six forms are transmitted from the readers. There are also four forms reported from the Arabs: "'alayhumi" with a damma on the ha' and a kasra on the mim, with a ya' inserted; "'alayhum" with a damma on the ha' and a kasra on the mim without an added ya'; "'alayhimu" with a kasra on the ha' and a damma on the mim without an added waw; and "'alayhimi" with a kasra on the ha' and the mim, with no ya' after the mim.

As for "those who have earned anger" (al-maghdub 'alayhim), they are the Jews; and "those who have gone astray" (al-dallin), they are the Christians.

This was narrated by 'Adi ibn Hatim from the Prophet ﷺ.

Ibn Qutaybah said: Al-dalal (ḍalāl) is bewilderment and deviation from the truth.

Section

It is from the Sunnah, with regard to the one who recites al-Fatihah, that he follow it with "Amin" (āmīn). Our shaykh Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn 'Ubayd Allah said: This applies whether he is outside the prayer or within it, on the basis of what Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "When the imam says ﴿Not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray﴾, then say from behind him 'Amin,' for whoever's saying coincides with the saying of the people of the heavens, his previous sins will be forgiven."

Regarding the meaning of "Amin," there are three opinions.

The first: that the meaning of "Amin" is: "Thus let it be." This was related by Ibn al-Anbari from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan.

The second: that it means: "O Allah, answer." This was said by al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj.

The third: that it is one of the names of Allah the Exalted. This was said by Mujahid, Hilal ibn Yasaf, and Ja'far ibn Muhammad.

Ibn Qutaybah said: Its meaning is "O Amin, answer our supplication," and the "ya" was dropped, as it was dropped in His saying: ﴿Yusuf, turn away from this﴾ [Yusuf: 29], meaning "O Yusuf." As for one who lengthens the alif and says "Amin," he has added the alif of address to the alif of "Amin," as it is said "Azayd, come forward," meaning "O Zayd." Ibn al-Anbari said: This view is in error according to all the grammarians, because if "ya" were prefixed to "Amin" it would be a singular vocative, whose final letter would take the nominative; since the Arabs have unanimously given its nun a fatha, this shows it is not a vocative. Rather, the nun of "Amin" is fathah because it and the ya' before it are sukun, as the Arabs say "layta" and "la'alla." He said: There are two dialects for "Amin": "Amin" with a short vowel (qasr), and "Amin" with a long vowel (madd), and the nun is fathah in both.

Abu al-Abbas recited to us from Ibn al-A'rabi:

Allah give drink to a living place between Sarah and al-Hima (ḥimá), near Fayd, under the rain of the cloud-bearing showers.
Amin, and may Allah bring a company to them with goodness, and guard them from the death-fate of the desert.

Abu al-Abbas also recited:

Far from me has departed a great stallion and his maternal cousin; Amin, and may Allah increase the distance between us.

Abu al-Abbas also recited:

O Lord, do not deprive me of her love ever, and may Allah have mercy on a servant who says "amina."

Ubayy recited to me:

Amin, and whoever has given you from me a kindness, may Allah cast into his limbs and he will be stiffened.

Ubayy also recited to me:

I said to him: You have stirred up for me the lightning of longing; may the death-fate strike the one of us who is less in grief.
Amin, and longing has afflicted him beyond what he bears, and he has suffered from its torments hardship.

Section

Most of them reported from Ahmad that al-Fatihah is a condition for the validity of the prayer; whoever abandons it while able to recite it, his prayer is not valid. This is also the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is not specifically required. This is also a narration from Ahmad. What supports the first narration is what is recorded in the two Sahihs from the hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "There is no prayer for one who does not recite the Opening of the Book."

And Allah knows best what is correct.
